{{short description|Russian mathematician}}
'''Anatoli''' '''Nikolaievich Andrianov''' (also spelled '''Anatoly'''; {{Langx|ru|Анатолий Николаевич Андрианов}}; 21 July 1936 – 2 May 2020)<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=Andrianov, Anatolij N. - Deutsche Biographie |url=https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/gnd138533121.html |access-date=2026-08-19 |website=www.deutsche-biographie.de |language=de}}</ref> is a Russian mathematician.

Andrianov received in 1962 his Ph.D. under [[Yuri Linnik]] at the [[Saint Petersburg State University|Leningrad State University]] with thesis ''Investigation of quadratic forms by methods of the theory of correspondences''<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=87328|name=Anatoli N. Andrianov}}</ref> and in 1969 his Russian doctorate of sciences ([[Doctor Nauk]]).<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://library.ias.edu/files/pdfs/hs/cos.pdf |title=A Community of Scholars, Institute for Advanced Study, Faculty and Members 1930–1980 |access-date=2016-06-29 |archive-date=2017-11-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171107021042/https://library.ias.edu/files/pdfs/hs/cos.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> He is a professor at the [[Steklov Institute]] in [[Saint Petersburg]].

His research deals with the multiplicative arithmetic of quadratic forms, zeta functions of automorphic forms, modular forms in several variables (such as  Siegel modular forms, [[Hecke operator]]s, spherical functions, and [[theta function]]s).

Andrianov was an Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] in 1970 in Nice with talk ''On the zeta function of the general linear group'' and in 1983 in Warsaw with talk ''Integral representation of quadratic forms by quadratic forms: multiplicative properties''.<ref>Andrianov, A. N. [http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1983.1/Main/icm1983.1.0465.0474.ocr.pdf "Integral representations of quadratic forms by quadratic forms: multiplicative properties."] In Proc. Intern. Congress of Mathematicians, Warsaw (1983), vol. 1, pp. 465–474. 1983.</ref> He held visiting positions at several academic institutions, including the [[Max Planck Institute for Mathematics]] in Bonn, at the Institut Fourier in [[Grenoble]] and at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] (1974).
